REFERRAL LETTER
Date: 11/26/2026
Patient Name: Thomas Fowler
DOB: 06/19/1942
MRN: MRN-43830

To: Cardiology Clinic Intake
From: Dr. Alan Carter, TriCounty Medical Practice

Dear Colleague,

Reason for referral: Evaluation of persistent fatigue with a strong family history of early heart disease.

Thomas Fowler is an 84-year-old man followed at TriCounty Medical Practice. His history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypothyroidism. For several months, he has had reduced energy that limits his usual activities.

His father had a heart attack in his early 50s, and his older brother developed heart disease before age 55. I would appreciate your assessment of his persistent fatigue in light of this strong family history of early heart disease.

Thank you for seeing this patient.

Dr. Alan Carter
TriCounty Medical Practice

Provider: Dr. Alan Carter

SUBJECTIVE:
Thomas Fowler returns for routine follow-up of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hypothyroidism. He reports taking his established treatment consistently and has no new concerns.

VITALS:
BP 143/81, HR 87, RR 14, SpO2 98% on room air, weight 163 lb.

EXAM:
General: comfortable at rest.
Neck: supple, no jugular venous distension.
Cardiac exam: regular rate and rhythm, normal S1 and S2, soft systolic murmur at the sternal border, no gallop.
Lungs: clear bilaterally.
Extremities: no peripheral edema.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Hypertension is stable by history. Continue established treatment, track blood pressure at home, limit dietary salt, and remain physically active.
2. Type 2 diabetes is stable by history. Continue the established care plan, follow a balanced meal plan, stay active, and track glucose at home.
3. Hypothyroidism is stable by history. Continue established treatment and report new fatigue, cold intolerance, or bowel changes.

ADMISSION DIAGNOSIS:
Thomas Fowler, an 84-year-old male, was admitted for acute diverticulitis with abdominal discomfort and reduced appetite. The working diagnosis was based on his symptoms and the overall clinical assessment. His illness was managed without an operation. At admission, the care team reviewed his known hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypothyroidism as part of planning supportive care. The immediate goals were to reduce abdominal symptoms, maintain hydration, and observe for any worsening or complication. He was able to participate in discussion of the plan, and his family was kept informed with his permission. The admission was limited to treatment of the acute intestinal illness and coordination of a safe transition home. No calendar dates, medication names, test names, or numerical results are included in this summary. The course described below reflects a gradual response to nonoperative care.

The focus was on comfort, hydration, and limiting intestinal strain while his symptoms were active. He was asked to report whether abdominal discomfort was changing and whether he could tolerate fluids. The care team reviewed the plan with him and answered questions about the expected recovery. His appetite remained reduced early in the course, so food intake was advanced cautiously rather than forced. The possibility of operative treatment was considered in the context of his overall progress, but there was no indication to proceed with surgery during this admission. His chronic conditions remained part of the care plan. The general surgery service reviewed the case and agreed that nonoperative management was appropriate while Mr. Fowler continued to improve. Their input supported ongoing observation and conservative treatment rather than an operation. The inpatient team coordinated care around the shared plan and kept the patient and family informed about what changes would require reassessment. No procedural intervention was recommended during the stay. Other members of the care team assisted with nutrition planning, mobility as tolerated, and preparation for a safe return home. The patient’s chronic hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypothyroidism were considered in discharge coordination, with routine ongoing care left to his established clinicians. No medication names, doses, named tests, imaging findings, numerical results, physical examination findings, or vital signs are recorded in this section. PROCEDURES:
No operative procedure was performed during this admission. Mr. Fowler’s diverticulitis was managed with conservative measures, observation, hydration, symptom relief, and antimicrobial therapy. The decision to avoid surgery was consistent with his improving symptoms and the recommendations of the general surgery service. No invasive intervention was required to support the inpatient course. Care focused on allowing a gradual return to oral intake and maintaining a safe level of comfort while discharge arrangements were completed. The patient and family were informed that no procedure had been undertaken and were given guidance on seeking reassessment if symptoms returned or worsened. This section contains no named medication, dose, diagnostic test, imaging result, numerical value, physical examination finding, or vital sign. His recovery plan remained centered on supportive care and continued follow-up after leaving the hospital.

CONDITION AT DISCHARGE:
At discharge, Mr. Fowler had improved abdominal symptoms and was taking fluids and food sufficiently to continue recovery at home. He did not require an operation during the admission. He was considered appropriate for discharge with family support and instructions for a gradual return to his usual routine. The patient understood that improvement may continue over several days and that a recurrence or worsening of symptoms should prompt contact with a clinician. His hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypothyroidism remained relevant chronic conditions for routine outpatient management. No physical examination findings or vital signs are included in this summary. No named medication, dose, test, imaging finding, laboratory value, or calendar date is stated. The discharge decision was based on his overall progress, ability to manage oral intake, and the availability of a follow-up plan.
Thomas Fowler | MRN-43830 | Discharge summary | Page 11 of 12

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
Mr. Fowler was advised to advance his diet gradually as tolerated and maintain regular fluid intake. He should avoid foods that clearly worsen his symptoms during the early recovery period and return to his usual eating pattern as comfort allows. He was asked to rest as needed while resuming ordinary activity in stages. He should seek prompt medical attention for worsening abdominal pain, persistent inability to eat or drink, repeated vomiting, new fever, faintness, or any other marked change. He and his family were instructed to contact his established care team if recovery does not continue as expected. Chronic care for hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypothyroidism should continue through the existing care plan. No medication names, doses, or changes are provided in this summary. The patient and family confirmed understanding of these instructions before leaving the hospital.

Transthoracic echo this admission: LVEF 30%. Mild left atrial enlargement. Severely reduced left ventricular systolic function.
Thomas Fowler | MRN-43830 | Discharge summary | Page 12 of 12

FOLLOW-UP:
Mr. Fowler should arrange follow-up with his established primary care clinician after discharge to review recovery from diverticulitis and continue routine care of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypothyroidism. He should also follow any guidance provided by the general surgery service if symptoms recur or if further review is advised. The timing should be coordinated with his outpatient clinicians based on his progress and access to care. He should bring a summary of the hospitalization to those appointments and describe any ongoing abdominal discomfort, changes in appetite, or difficulty maintaining fluids. His family may assist with arranging transportation and keeping track of follow-up plans. If symptoms worsen before a scheduled appointment, he should seek prompt medical attention rather than wait. No calendar date, medication name, dose, test, imaging result, or numerical value is included. The plan is for continued recovery at home without an operation.
